data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Accepting the defensibility of preference costs the objectivity of scientific progress, reducing it to a convention of 'critical rationalism' that cannot distinguish itself from dogmatism in the limit.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper is a realist who believes truth exists independently of our methods, this conventionalist reading misrepresents him.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'cost' is acceptable because objectivity lies in the method, not the result, the position remains stable.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference can be grounded in the logical content (information richness) of the theory rather than its history, the loss of objectivity is mitigated.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"If corroboration is not probability, and preference is merely a rule of thumb for error avoidance, then there is no objective sense in which the preferred theory is 'better' than a rival that hasn't been tested yet, except that it has survived so far. This makes the preference a convention. The cost is that we cannot claim science objectively progresses toward truth; we only claim it adheres to a specific set of rules (the critical method). If a dogmatist refuses to test their theory, Popper can only say they are violating the rules, not that they are objectively wrong about the world. The 'survival' of the view depends on accepting conventionalism over realism.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
